In a contextual-stress control, tag-scoped writer inputs remove detected out-of-scope anchor copying. Frozen questions authored on staged dossiers transfer less reliably to one-pass dossiers of the same states. In matched evidence controls, whole sections repair 29 of 32 GPT-5.1 and 25 of 30 Sonnet 4.6 failures labeled as packaging, compared with 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. Attribution uses separate key-based and key-free support measures, with model disagreements retained. Length remains confounded with persona and question composition; the observed between-bucket widening depends on excerpt construction. The benchmark supports offline evaluation against known facts. Memory acquisition from interaction and validation against real users remain outside its scope.

papers.title: Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies
papers.abstract: AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.

papers.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
papers.abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

papers.title: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are commonly pretrained with likelihood-based objectives such as masked language modeling or denoising. These objectives capture sequence-level regularities, but can produce representations in which functional signals are entangled with non-functional variation (e.g., sequence identity, compositional bias, and frequent local motifs), creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction. We introduce Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (SAVR), a contrastive post-training method using Pfam family co-membership as a homology-guided discrete semantic signal to reshape PLM representations. SAVR reduces directional dominance and redistributes variance across embedding dimensions, decreasing variance concentration, and increasing effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without observing any task-specific labels during post-training, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation. These results suggest that homology-guided contrastive post-training can rectify PLM representation geometry and improve sequence-based protein function prediction.

papers.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

papers.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
papers.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

papers.title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
papers.abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

papers.title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
papers.abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.

papers.title: Incorporating argumentation frameworks for LLM decision-making: Task-specific design and evaluation
papers.abstract: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.

papers.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

papers.title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

papers.title: FPGA-GEN: Target-Aware RTL Generation via HLS
papers.abstract: Successful C/C++ compilation does not guarantee correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS). FPGA-GEN is an agentic HLS-C generation workflow that encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules in explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops for candidate-level decisions. On HLS-Eval, five shared-context outputs per task yield 407/425 (95.8%) public-testbench passes. In a cumulative conversion campaign, FPGA-GEN admits 104/107 (97.2%) HLS-LeVeri designs under held-out co-simulation, Vivado synthesis/fit, and same-RTL evidence. In focused TensorCore screening, selected candidate 3 reports 73.7% fewer CSynth cycles and 14.6% fewer LUTs than generated/composed C0, with 26.7% more DSPs, and passes development CoSim.

papers.title: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware
papers.abstract: As LLM agents increasingly generate RTL alongside the tests and reviews that validate it, self-generated evidence is a weak foundation for trustworthy hardware. We present our seven-stage verification-gated workflow, evolved during a post-quantum design port, in which a gate counts only if shown able to fail on negative controls and fault mutants, and reviewer agents audit work before commit. We then audit this evidence with tool-selected netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. The flow ported an ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator to a 300 MHz Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card: all six operations are byte-exact on the board, and it passes all 85 interface-applicable NIST ACVP cases (of 285) and 484 ML-DSA known answers. However, passing module tests overstate the verification strength. Across three RTL modules, existing simulation gates kill only 76% of 399 tool-selected netlist mutants; specification-derived tests guided by the survivors raise the fresh-draw decapsulation kill rate from 48% to 74%. In pre-registered single-model replays on flaws invisible to known-answer tests, undirected whole-design review catches two verifier flaws in only 3/6 and 1/6 sessions, whereas module-scoped review catches every known flaw in all 54 sessions. Even scoped review detects planted key-custody flaws in only 3/20 sessions, whereas formal checks (one added for the replay) flag every one. In this study, trustworthy agentic hardware needed author-independent mutants for test gates, module-level scoping for LLM review, and formal checks for custody invariants.

papers.title: ReLay: Bidirectional Layout-Code Translation and Library Evolution for Reusable and Process-Portable Analog Design
papers.abstract: Analog layout generators provide a programmable interface for design reuse and process migration, but their coverage is limited by handcrafted libraries. The designer knowledge embedded in complete layouts remains implicit in their geometry, making it difficult to capture in reusable generator libraries. We present ReLay, a bidirectional layout-code framework that recovers generator programs from existing layouts, enabling cross-PDK portability and parametric resizing of existing designs. Constructions that recur across recovered programs are promoted to library functions, so the library evolves as layouts accumulate. We also introduce the first layout-code benchmark: 1,050 hand-drawn layouts from 27 circuit families across three open-source PDKs, ranging from primitive cells to full chips. Learned functions account for 53-66% of layout-building calls in held-out layouts, demonstrating reuse beyond the learning corpus. Frontier LLM agents use ReLay to produce new layouts at 64-77% lower API cost per completed task than direct geometry generation, with comparable completion rates and electrical quality.

papers.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
papers.abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.

papers.title: VoxForge: A Unified Foundation Model for Dense 3D Features Across MRI, CT and PET
papers.abstract: A unified 3D medical foundation model promises reusable, frozen features that serve a wide variety of tasks such as segmentation, classification and registration on MRI, CT and PET as well as specialist models do. Generalist models still need separate backbones for localized and global tasks, specialist models are confined to a single modality, with the concern that spanning modalities under-emphasizes fine anatomy, and both typically rely on end-to-end fine-tuning to be competitive. We present VoxForge, a single encoder that integrates recent advances in 3D architecture, self-distillation and cross-modal curricula to learn transferable features from permissively licensed MRI and CT volumes. We evaluate it strictly frozen, the test a reusable foundation model must pass, against state-of-the-art generalist and specialist models on segmentation, classification and registration across MRI and CT, and on PET, which it never sees. VoxForge has the best or tied-best average rank in every task group, serves localized and global tasks across modalities at the level of state-of-the-art specialists, and is extremely label-efficient, matching top-performing models on TotalSegmentator CT with a tenth of the labels.
